"We must come to terms with a civilisation -- the Persian civilisation -- which is millennia-old and combines doctrine and religious faith, the concept of jihad as an armed struggle to the point of ultimate sacrifice, as well as death for one's country and religion," states Cardinal Sako. "The way of thinking and reasoning," he warns, "is different, and this is where the question arises as to how it is possible to establish a dialogue. And the answer is neither easy nor immediate." When discussing Iran, it is essential to understand that "we are not merely dealing with a political phenomenon; we must also take the religious dimension into account. And this element is absent in the West." "In our Eastern world," he adds, "priority is often tied to religion, unlike in the West, where politics and economic interests usually prevail." As has been observed on several occasions in the past, in this sense Christians (and the Church) can play a fundamental role as a bridge between the two cultures, between the two hemispheres of the globe which often struggle to communicate and understand one another: "Peace is not achieved through weapons!"

Patriarch for the whole of Iraq

During his 13 years at the helm of the Chaldean Patriarchate -- one of the oldest rites of the Eastern Church but deeply linked to Rome and the Pope -- there has been no shortage of challenges and dramatic moments, starting with the tragedy of ISIS, which "affected me deeply: their rise has undoubtedly been the most significant event in the recent history of Iraq and its Christians", with the displacement of hundreds of thousands of people in Mosul and the Nineveh Plain. In recent years, a slow process of reconstruction has begun, which is struggling to ensure security and stability despite the efforts of the Church and the Iraqi government, rendering calls for the return of the diaspora communities futile so far. A veritable exodus which, since 2003 following the US invasion and the fall of Saddam Hussein, has led to a collapse in the Christian population, which has fallen from 1.3 million to fewer than 400,000 today. And it is to them that the cardinal's thoughts turn. "Before talking about a return [as promised by the Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi to Patriarch Mar Paul III Nona, the cardinal's successor, at a meeting on 11 July]," observes Sako, "we must examine the conditions that drove Christians to leave."

Lasting stability, an environment in which people can live in peace even if they have lost faith in the possibility of achieving it; the prevalence of sectarian affiliations and divisions over the concepts of citizenship and justice; the lack of compensation for damage caused by Daesh [the Arabic acronym for ISIS] and Christian property confiscated by militias, which has not been returned; the spread of corruption; and the deterioration of essential services are just some of the many unresolved issues. "There is a lack of job prospects," he continues, "as well as infrastructure, schools, services and hospitals. Christians will not return unless the culture and laws change, with the establishment of a state founded on citizenship rather than on confessional divisions, and with a reform of the laws. In particular," explains the Patriarch Emeritus, "those relating to the Islamisation of minors and the appropriation of their rights and property. Furthermore, there is still a continuous exodus due to emigration. These are central, and unresolved, issues!"

Security, employment, services and the fight against "endemic corruption" are areas that affect the entire population and Iraq as a whole, a nation -- the cardinal reiterates once again -- that should "base its reconstruction on the value of citizenship". "In many of my speeches," recalls Cardinal Sako, "I have spoken not only on behalf of and to Christians, but also to Muslims, calling for the separation of religion from the state, and for the creation of common ground where all citizens enjoy equal dignity and their rights are respected." He then recalls the significant work carried out in favour of Islamic-Christian dialogue, which "has made great strides in recent years" and is evidenced by meetings with Sunni, Shia and Kurdish authorities, starting with Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani, the most important Shia Muslim leader in the Arab country, "whom I have visited twice in Najaf". "Thanks to these efforts," he observes, "and to the relationships built up over time, we have been able to put an end to hate speech. Christians are no longer spoken ill of in the mosques!" "The only thing that struck me and caused me pain," he adds with a note of bitterness, "is the withdrawal of the patriarchal decree issued by the then-president Abdul Latif Rashid, behind which lay the manoeuvring and interests of a so-called Christian militia. However, I have always refused to have Christian militias or sectarian militias." "Before appealing to Christians to return," he emphasises, "the Church must help those Christians who have remained, and give them hope."

The Challenges Facing the Church

Having recently returned to Iraq after attending the last consistory convened by Pope Leo XIV at the end of June, the cardinal then turns his attention to the universal Church and the future of the mission. "The recent synodal experience," he says, "has been a source of satisfaction, because we in the East have been living it for some time. The Synod is a place and an opportunity for working together, for studying problems and challenges, desires and plans, and for making decisions together. This is the Church born of the pontificate of Pope Francis, who emphasised the theme of synodality, of walking together. This aspect is very positive." And regarding his successor, Pope Leo XIV, he says he appreciates his speeches, which are "brief and to the point, using language that speaks to the people. Pope Leo is no longer the head of a dicastery of the Roman Curia, but is the father and shepherd of the entire Catholic Church.

"I hope," he adds, "that his message is for everyone, not just for the West, because we need to speak to the whole world. And his apostolate is not just for Christians, but for everyone when he calls for peace, coexistence and dignity, and for how to engage with other religions, especially Islam."

In an age characterised by speed, the internet and artificial intelligence, in which the Church risks appearing 'slow' and 'wasting' time, he urges us to find new ways forward and 'immediate responses' capable of speaking to today's society. 'It is necessary,' he reflects, 'to seek an approach based on dialogue. People do not accept being guided as mere subjects. We bishops are fathers and shepherds; we must know how to understand them and adopt a style of paternal and fraternal dialogue." As for the Chaldean community, which is getting to know his successor, Patriarch Nona, the cardinal reiterates once more that he "will not comment on the direction or decisions taken, but will remain discreet. My time," he emphasises, "has come to an end, and now a new phase begins." "Every day," the cardinal confides, "I pray for the Patriarch, for the bishops, but above all for the Chaldean Church, which is and remains a MARTYRED Church that has much to offer the universal Church in terms of liturgy, spirituality and biblical pastoral care -- not merely scholastic or philosophical." And as for Iraq and its Christians, the cardinal concludes, "I am sure that the situation will change for the better; there will be full religious freedom and the Chaldean community will continue to grow. I pray for this."

Lisa’s turn loop 👇

I'm going to assume anyone reading this knows what a turn loop is. If not, hey, follow me on LinkedIn! 😆

🔁 The loop always has an active mode that determines its instructions, available capabilities, and execution policy. A mode handoff is a state transition—it changes that working context while preserving conversation evidence. The model can request the transition, but the harness performs it.

🔀 Within a turn, the model chooses whether to request tools, hand off, ask for input, or offer a final answer. The harness handles those requests under explicit policies. It can also force a handoff, request intervention, pause, or terminate on its own. Operator commands can pause, stop, or terminate execution.

 🔂 These lifecycle outcomes are explicit, typed actions—not just different reasons to break out of a loop. Iteration and tool-call budgets, handoff limits, and stall detection govern when execution must change course. Completion checks distinguish supported success from an unverified claim. Asking for help, exhausting a budget, and finishing the work are distinctly different outcomes.

🧭 Lisa reconstructs workflow progress from its durable conversation log, including plans and completion evidence, so remaining work can be recovered across turns and restarts. Where a mode requires a write, completion checks look for recorded effect receipts rather than accepting the model’s success claim alone.

ℹ️ The same loop supports changing roles, multi-step plans, parallel work, recovery, and operator control. The model supplies flexible reasoning; the kernel governs execution and checks completion evidence.

So the idea that the turn loop is a simple 3-state FSM is now just a memory; it's gotten a little more complicated over time, @JoshARosen, but à la explicit actions, I'd still call it FSM-based. 😊

A software developer is approached on a regular job platform by someone posing as another company. After two fake interviews, he is asked to download a coding assignment. It contains malware that security systems do not initially catch.

OCT 20
Through the compromised computer and an internal AI tool, the attackers reach the devices of two more wallet-team employees. They find credentials that let them install their own programs inside Binance's infrastructure.

OCT 29
They use that access to run a manipulated program and reach the internal service that signs wallet transactions. Then comes the twist: using Ethereum's EIP-7702, they give a smart contract they control execution rights over a Binance hot wallet, bypassing the normal withdrawal system.

This explains why the transfers kept flowing even after regular withdrawals were halted. The on-chain permissions had to be revoked separately.

The key detail: according to the findings so far, the attackers did not steal the private keys. They manipulated the infrastructure around them.

THE DAMAGE AND THE RECOVERY
• About $6.34B left several hot wallets within hours, including 18,270 BTC
• Binance says it froze roughly $2.85B with help from analytics firms and stablecoin issuers
• It says it will cover all losses and that 98% of affected holdings were restocked by October 31
• Withdrawals are back, and per Binance's founder, customers at times deposited more than they withdrew

WHO IS BEHIND IT?
• TRM Labs traces it to North Korean actors, citing links to earlier attacks such as the Bitget hack
• The FBI officially attributes it to North Korea, under the label "TraderTraitor"
• Binance says it prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked attacks this year

North Korea denies it. Kim Yo-jong called the US claims "absurd rhetoric" and suggested that whoever receives the recovered crypto might be the one behind it, pointing to US plans to use seized crypto for a strategic reserve. She offered no evidence.

Worth noting: seized assets should go back to their rightful owners, not automatically to a state. And $6.3B is roughly 20% of North Korea's annual economic output, which gives Pyongyang its own financial motive.

WHAT TO TAKE AWAY
This was not a smart contract bug or a stolen password. It was patient social engineering aimed at the people who hold the keys to the system.

Binance says it has closed the gaps, rebuilt affected systems, tightened device security and commissioned an independent investigation.

The denial does not change the findings published so far.

The biggest myth about U.S. aid to Israel is finally collapsing. https://t.co/bMkS0gZYyE 
On Tuesday morning, as Americans headed to the polls for their midterm elections, President Donald Trump made a massive announcement: The United States would stop providing nearly $4 billion in annual military aid to the Jewish state by the end of 2026.

For decades, such an announcement would have been treated as a diplomatic catastrophe. Israeli politicians would have rushed to Washington, American Jewish organizations would have mobilized, and commentators would have warned that the future of the Jewish state was suddenly in jeopardy.

But President Trump just did Israel an enormous favor.

Certainly, $4 billion is not an insignificant amount of money. American military assistance has been incredibly important to Israel’s security. And the United States and Israel should not become less friendly. But the end of American military aid could be one of the most important steps toward completing the promise of Israeli independence.

For nearly 80 years, the Jewish state has been building toward a moment when it could finally look the world’s greatest superpower in the eye and say something that Jews, for most of their history, were rarely in a position to say to anyone: Thank you. We can take care of ourselves.

Under the existing agreement, Israel receives approximately $3.8 billion annually, including $3.3 billion in Foreign Military Financing and $500 million for cooperative missile defense. The foreign military financing is overwhelmingly directed toward purchasing American-made military equipment. By 2028, the special provision allowing Israel to spend some of that financing on its own defense industry is scheduled to disappear entirely.

In other words, much of the money Americans supposedly “give” Israel is money Israel must spend in America.

It supports American manufacturers, American workers, American military production, and American technological capabilities. The United States also benefits from intelligence cooperation, joint research, access to Israeli innovation, and military technologies refined under conditions that American forces do not ordinarily experience.

There is Trophy, the Israeli-developed active protection system adopted by the U.S. Army for its Abrams tanks; or the Israeli expertise incorporated into the F-35’s advanced helmet-mounted display system.

The relationship has never been simply one country giving and another receiving. Both sides have gained enormously. And yet, every American election cycle, Israel finds itself portrayed as a helpless foreign dependent draining the American treasury.

That perception is not only misleading. It has become strategically and politically damaging.

Some Americans wonder why they should continue financing another country’s military. But Israelis should be asking an equally important question: What exactly are we sacrificing in exchange for that money?

Because the assistance has never been free.

When a country becomes accustomed to having another government finance a significant portion of its military procurement, the arrangement inevitably shapes its decisions. It influences which weapons it purchases, where those weapons are manufactured, which technologies receive investment, and how much of its defense infrastructure it can build at home.

The current agreement, negotiated under President Barack Obama in 2016, committed $38 billion over 10 years. It also accelerated the phasing out of Israel’s ability to spend American military financing on products manufactured in Israel.

Think about the implications. A country that has developed some of the most sophisticated military technology on Earth has been operating under a system that increasingly directs its military purchasing power toward foreign manufacturers rather than its own.

To be fair, American financing has also freed Israeli resources for indigenous research and development, helping Israel build capabilities that benefit both nations. But that advantage comes alongside a genuine cost: a procurement system that reinforces dependence on foreign production.

And manufacturing dependence is only part of the problem. Military assistance gives Washington considerable leverage over Israeli decision-making. A delayed shipment, a threatened restriction, or a disagreement over how Israel conducts a military operation can suddenly become a question of national security.

American presidents, both Democratic and Republican, have understandably used that leverage to advance American interests. They are elected to serve the United States, not Israel. But Israel’s leaders are elected to serve Israel. Those interests frequently overlap, but they are not identical. What Washington considers prudent may be dangerous from Jerusalem’s perspective. What Americans can afford to postpone for another six months may be something Israelis believe they must confront tomorrow.

Israel should listen carefully to its allies, especially the United States. But there is an enormous difference between listening to a friend and being dependent on that friend’s approval. A country responsible for the survival of its own people cannot afford to confuse the two
To understand why this matters so much, we have to remember what Zionism was actually meant to accomplish.

For centuries, Jews lived at the mercy of rulers, governments, empires, and societies over which they had little control. Their security often depended on whether the people in power were friendly, indifferent, or hostile to them. Sometimes Jews prospered. Sometimes they enjoyed remarkable freedom. Sometimes they were welcomed, protected, and even celebrated. And sometimes everything changed.

The lesson of Jewish history is not that every non-Jewish government will betray us. It is that a people who cannot ultimately provide for their own security are always vulnerable to the decisions of others. That was one of Zionism’s most fundamental insights.

The Jewish People did not spend generations struggling to reestablish sovereignty in our ancestral homeland simply to replace dependence on European kings and foreign governments with dependence on American congressional appropriations. We wanted something far more meaningful than a powerful benefactor. We wanted the ability to determine our own future.

And remarkably, Israel’s history demonstrates that this was possible long before American military assistance became central to its defense establishment. In 1948, when the newly declared State of Israel faced invasion, the United States did not rush to supply it with advanced weapons. Washington maintained an arms embargo, and Israel had to find equipment wherever it could.

In the years that followed, France became one of Israel’s most important military suppliers. Then, just before the Six-Day War in 1967, French President Charles de Gaulle imposed an arms embargo of his own. Israel won that war anyway. And it is worth remembering that Israel’s greatest achievements did not come from the luxury of having every resource it needed. They came from a national determination to survive, regardless of whether the outside world was willing to help.

That determination helped produce an extraordinary military, a sophisticated intelligence community, a world-class technology sector, and one of the most innovative societies on Earth. Why should a country built on that spirit continue to organize so much of its national security around foreign assistance?

The Israel of 2026 is not the Israel of 1948.

In 1948, Israel was an impoverished newborn state absorbing Holocaust survivors and Jewish refugees from across the world, surrounded by enemies and desperately trying to acquire the basic tools of national survival.

Today, Israel is a country of more than 10 million people, with a highly developed economy, globally competitive technology companies, sophisticated universities, major financial institutions, and defense industries whose products are purchased around the world.

The Israeli economy is approaching $720 billion in 2026. The annual $3.8 billion assistance package represents only about half of one percent of that total, although it remains a meaningful sum within Israel’s defense budget.

More revealingly, Israel’s defense exports reached a record $19.2 billion in new agreements in 2025, nearly 30 percent higher than the previous year. The same country that American politicians routinely describe as a recipient of roughly $4 billion in military aid is signing almost five times that amount in annual defense export agreements.

Countries across Europe and Asia are purchasing Israeli missile defense systems, surveillance technology, radar, electronic warfare capabilities, and other advanced equipment because they recognize that Israel has developed technologies their own militaries need.

And beyond defense, American companies are investing staggering sums in Israeli innovation. Just this year, eight Israeli companies have been acquired for a combined $22 billion. In 2025, the combined value of several high-profile Israeli exits was $72 billion, including Google’s $29.5-billion acquisition of Wiz and Palo Alto Networks’ $25-billion acquisition of CyberArk.

An economy capable of producing that kind of value should have the confidence to rethink a military assistance arrangement designed for a much poorer and more vulnerable country. Israel is no longer merely a country that needs advanced military technology. It is one of the countries the world turns to for advanced military technology.

That is an extraordinary transformation, and Israel’s relationship with the United States should reflect it.

There is another reason why ending military aid should not be confused with abandoning the American-Israeli alliance: The United States has compelling reasons to maintain that alliance even without annual assistance.

Israel provides intelligence, technological innovation, military expertise, and a capable regional partner in one of the most strategically important parts of the world. The United States benefits from Israeli capabilities developed under the pressure of real-world threats. Israel benefits from American technology, military production, diplomatic cooperation, and access to the world’s largest economy.

Neither country needs to pretend that this relationship is a charitable enterprise. In fact, replacing military assistance with a more conventional commercial and strategic partnership could make the relationship healthier.

Israel can purchase American aircraft, ammunition, and other military equipment because those products serve its interests. American companies can purchase Israeli defense technology because those products serve theirs. Both governments can invest in joint research and development, cooperate on missile defense, share intelligence, and establish long-term industrial agreements.

The key is that each side should clearly understand what it contributes and what it receives.

Of course, paying for American weapons would not eliminate every form of dependence. Export approvals, production bottlenecks, and access to replacement parts would still matter. Israel will continuously need to develop domestic manufacturing, stockpiles, and alternative supply chains to achieve greater strategic autonomy. But those are arguments for a responsible transition, not permanent dependence.

An alliance becomes stronger when each country is respected for what it brings to the table, rather than defined by what one gives the other. The United States should want an Israel that is economically prosperous, militarily powerful, technologically advanced, and capable of defending itself. And Israel should want exactly the same thing.

For American Jews, there is another important benefit to ending the aid arrangement. They have watched Israel become a convenient political punching bag in debates that often have very little to do with Israel.
Whenever American politicians want to demonstrate their opposition to foreign spending, Israel’s aid package becomes an easy target. Whenever activists want to portray the United States as complicit in everything Israel does, the same $4 billion becomes their favorite talking point. And whenever conspiracy theorists want to claim that Jews somehow control American foreign policy, the aid package becomes their supposed evidence.

The fact that American interests benefit from the arrangement is rarely mentioned. Neither is the fact that much of the military financing is spent in the United States. Instead, the public is offered a deeply distorted image: The American taxpayer works, the Jewish state collects, and American politicians supposedly have little choice in the matter.

Ending the assistance would not end antisemitism. People determined to hate Jews have always found reasons, and they will undoubtedly find new ones. But it would remove one of the most convenient political instruments used to portray Israel as a burden on American society. More importantly, it would change the conversation about what supporting Israel actually means.

For too long, many American Jewish organizations have treated preserving the annual assistance package as one of the defining objectives of pro-Israel advocacy. But support for Israel should not be measured by how much money American taxpayers send to Jerusalem. It should be measured by whether Israel is becoming safer, stronger, more prosperous, more independent, and better positioned to secure the Jewish future. If ending military assistance advances those objectives over the long term, American Jews should welcome it.

There is something liberating about imagining a future in which Jewish communities in America no longer have to organize political campaigns around persuading their fellow citizens to finance another country’s defense. They can advocate for strong diplomatic relations, expanded economic cooperation, technological partnerships, and the shared interests that make the American-Israeli relationship valuable.

And, perhaps most importantly, they can return more of their attention to building vibrant Jewish communities, strengthening Jewish education, and deepening the connection between Jews in America and Israel.

The Jewish People have a history that stretches back thousands of years. Their relationship with the State of Israel should be considerably more meaningful than an annual debate over a line item in the American federal budget.

America has been an extraordinary friend to Israel, and American military support has contributed meaningfully to Israel’s security. Israelis should never forget the American leaders, soldiers, defense workers, and ordinary citizens who have stood with them.

Gratitude, however, is not the same as permanent dependence. In fact, the greatest compliment Israel can pay the United States is to demonstrate that decades of partnership helped create a country strong enough to stand increasingly on its own. And the greatest compliment America can pay Israel is to recognize that it has become that kind of country.

This is what makes Trump’s announcement so significant, regardless of the political calculations behind it. Less than eight decades after the establishment of a Jewish state in the aftermath of the Holocaust, the president of the world’s most powerful country is saying that the Jewish People have built a nation capable of taking responsibility for its own military purchases. That should be a tremendous source of Jewish pride.

It is easy to forget just how miraculous the existence of Israel really is. In the span of a few generations, a people who had been scattered across the world, repeatedly expelled, persecuted, and massacred built a sovereign country capable of defending itself, absorbing millions of immigrants, producing globally important technologies, and contributing to the security of other nations.

And now that country has the opportunity to take another meaningful step toward genuine independence. Independence means having friends without needing their permission to exist. It means making decisions based on the interests of your own citizens. It means building the capabilities to defend your country even when the international political environment turns against you. Above all, it means understanding that the ultimate responsibility for the survival of the Jewish state belongs to the Jewish state itself.

For generations, Jews dreamed of the day when their destiny would no longer be decided in foreign capitals. The establishment of Israel in 1948 made that dream a political reality. The extraordinary development of the country over the following decades made it an increasingly powerful reality. Now Israel has an opportunity to make it more complete.

The greatest gift America can give Israel is not another $4 billion. It is the chance for Israel to demonstrate that it no longer needs it. And a great achievement of the Jewish state would be to prove that President Trump is right.

text:
Someone smashed the statues and religious images inside a Catholic prayer hall in Israel, then left a handwritten note on the altar asking for forgiveness. The priest's response is rather extraordinary.

On Sunday, the Maronite Catholic community of Nahariya, in northern Israel, discovered that their prayer hall dedicated to Saints Peter and Paul had been vandalised. Statues lay shattered, sacred images had been damaged and a crucifix had been slashed. The community has a remarkable history, many are Lebanese Christians whose families fled into Israel following the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon in 2000. Some had served in the South Lebanon Army, which fought alongside Israel against Hezbollah. For more than a quarter of a century, these displaced Christians have maintained their faith and community in Nahariya. According to their priest, Fr Rudy Noura, nothing like this had happened to them before.

But amid the destruction, someone had left an extraordinary message on the altar. Addressed to the community, the handwritten note apologised for what had happened. Its author claimed not to understand what had driven them to commit the act and asked to be forgiven. Fr Noura's response was remarkable. Rather than speculate about the perpetrator's identity or motives, he spoke of someone who might be deeply troubled and in need of love. He said he was ready to forgive the person responsible. Meanwhile, Archbishop Moussa El-Hage, the Maronite Archbishop of Haifa, issued a strong condemnation of the desecration and demanded a proper investigation.

His statement contained a particularly important observation:

"Forgiveness does not mean remaining silent in the face of aggression, and love does not mean relinquishing our rights."

That strikes me as an excellent expression of the Catholic understanding of mercy.

Christian forgiveness does not require us to pretend that evil has not occurred, nor does it oblige victims to abandon their legitimate demand for justice. Indeed, genuine reconciliation requires truth, responsibility and, where appropriate, reparation.

We are commanded to love our enemies, but loving someone does not mean denying the seriousness of their actions. Justice and mercy are not competing virtues. Properly understood, they belong together.

There is also a broader question here about the protection of Christian communities in the Holy Land. Freedom of worship is not a privilege granted at the discretion of the majority. It is a fundamental human right, and authorities have a duty to protect the places where religious communities gather.

We do not yet know who committed this act or why. It would be irresponsible to attribute a religious or political motive before the investigation establishes the facts. Israeli police have opened an investigation, and officials have publicly condemned the attack. But the response of this small Maronite community deserves attention. They have suffered displacement, endured the upheavals of war and built a new life far from their ancestral homes. Now, confronted with the desecration of their place of prayer, their priest offers forgiveness while their archbishop insists upon justice.

There is something profoundly Christian about refusing both the temptation to hatred and the temptation to surrender one's rights.

May Saints Peter and Paul intercede for this community, and may those responsible find the courage to make amends.

text:
#Offerings film review

Here's an original story: A young boy is abused by his mother: a trashy, boozy, foul-mouthed, chain-smoking harridan. The boy endures her daily insults in silence. He never talks. Not to anyone. Not since dad "disappeared" (rumors vary). But at least Quiet Boy has a hobby -- he tortures small animals.

The neighborhood kids think Quiet Boy is retarded, and so they relate to him in the time-honored tradition of how children deal with the mentally handicapped: they tease him. They play pranks on him. And then ... one of those pranks "goes wrong."

Flashforward ten years.

Quiet Boy has spent the past decade institutionalized in an asylum, horribly disfigured from that childhood prank. Doctors think he's a vegetable. Never talks. But one night a nurse doesn't sedate him on schedule. It never mattered before. But on this, the ten year anniversary, Quiet Boy escapes. He treks forty miles to his hometown in search of his former tormentors (who've all blossomed into stunningly attractive high school seniors, looking too old for high school) and ... the body count mounts!

Of the many slasher films "inspired" by #Halloween (1978), Offerings is both a latecomer and one of the most slavishly unoriginal. Its ominous piano score sounds identical to #JohnCarpenter's. And its killer is an #Überpsycho, a dark avenging angel of superhuman strength and endurance. With one hand, he lifts a struggling victim off her feet. He tosses a noose around another victim and hauls him up the side of a house without trouble. He is shot several times, but continues relentlessly. A sign warns Danger! High Voltage, yet he grips the electric fence and climbs over.

(I coined Überpsycho in my essay, "But Is It Horror? Defining and Demarcating the Genre" to distinguish the indestructible post-Halloween "horror psycho" from the vulnerable "suspense psycho" of such earlier films as #Frenzy. For a fuller, more up-to-date analysis, see my book, Horror Film Aesthetics.)

(Blooper: the electric fence stands isolated. Aren't all "live" fences positioned between dead fences? Otherwise, innocent passersby, on either side, might mistakenly touch it.)

There are some clever deaths and attempts at black humor, and director #ChristopherReynolds can stretch a low budget. One victim is dragged under bed, his legs flailing, then shuddering, then the blood. That's one way to save on effects: hide the mayhem under bed. Another cost-saving method is to show a screaming head set to be split, then cut to its shadow as it's finally cracked. We hear only the head split, and see blood spattering the shadow. Not necessarily great art, but journeyman competence.

As in Halloween, there's the requisite good girl, Gretchen (#LorettaLeighBowman, who is pretty but lacks #JamieLeeCurtis's range and intensity). As a child, Gretchen was the one neighborhood kid who defended Quiet Boy. As an adolescent, Gretchen honors her parents, and says "no" to the boys.

Quiet Boy remembers Gretchen's kindness. As he butchers and slaughters his former tormentors (Gretchen's friends), he leaves their body parts on her porch -- his "offerings" of gratitude and love. (Don't worry: he doesn't just kill his former tormentors, but anyone in his path, so the body count is generous.)

Attempts at black humor include a finger eaten by a dog and pizza topped with human flesh. (A joke too stale to be funny.) Reynolds's broad range of levity also encompasses masturbation and porn jokes, and mocking the boob tube (another old film conceit). One dying boy flails outside the window as his parents watch TV, laughing at cartoons. Elsewhere, teenagers watch a horror film on TV, commenting on the characters' stupidity.

Playing off this "in joke," the characters in Offerings are just as dumb. After being knocked out, one teen awakes strapped upon a tool table, his head clamped in a steel vise (not very convincingly). He asks: "Hey, is this a joke? Very funny, guys. C'mon, at least loosen the straps."

Yeah, sure it's a joke. My friends are always braining each other, then strapping themselves under drill presses and before circular blades.

Despite following the Halloween blueprint, Offerings suffers from structural sloppiness. Quiet Boy is said to have cannibalized his mother (hence, the pizza toppings?). But when might he have eaten mom? She was fine before the prank, immediately after which Quiet Boy was institutionalized. Quite a plot hole.

Also, it's nighttime in Oklahoma when Gretchen's parents phone from Hawaii. Considering the time difference, and assuming it's May or June, the airport in "Hawaii" still looked too bright for evening. The shadows were long but distinct, and the sky was too bright. It looked like mid-morning in Hawaii and midnight in Oklahoma.

As in much low-budget exploitation indie fare, the lighting is flat, rather than atmospheric. And the no-name cast gives a mostly stilted performance (apart from two hams -- a gravedigger and a deputy). However, Offerings went the extra mile to offer night-for-night photography, always a plus in horror. And in addition to its Carpenter-like piano score, Offerings also has generic spacey musical effects, at times sounding like a 1950s sci-fi film. A peculiar choice, but nicely eerie.

The end credits indicate that Offerings was shot with some assistance from the #UniversityOfOklahoma's film department, and indeed, some of the film is shot on campus. Maybe this was a film school project? Offerings is woefully unoriginal compared to some of the work produced at the more prominent film schools at NYU, USC, UCLA, and AFI. Still, it's nice to see a film school take an interest in a feature length slasher film.

Choosy audiences will wish to decline these Offerings, but aficionados of low- budget indie horror should be more forgiving. Offerings delivers what it offers ... a generic but serviceable Überpsycho body-count film.

     -- written by Thomas M. Sipos, author of Horror Film Aesthetics: https://t.co/MoiAPAbWPM

Today I went to vote for my representative in Congress. There was one name on the ballot: Katherine Clark.

The job pays $174,000 a year and comes with considerable status. Massachusetts has about hundreds of thousands of unemployed people. There are a few million workers here who earn less than that salary. Tell me none of them would want the job.

Tell me you wouldn't take that job if all you had to do was show up.

A political system doesn’t have to abolish elections to abolish democracy. It only has to abolish competition. Keep the ritual of voting, remove the choice, and you’ve preserved the appearance of democracy while eliminating its purpose.

In 2024, five of our nine congressional races had a single name on the ballot. This year, the majority of state legislative seats were settled before anyone voted.

Whatever issue you care about, the outcome is decided by the people in office. A representative who never faces an opponent never has to defend a record, debate a rival, or persuade anyone to keep the job. 

There are many reasons races go uncontested, but some barriers are written into our rules, and they make it hard enough that most people never try. A congressional candidate needs 2,000 certified signatures. A candidate seeking either major party’s nomination also needs 15 percent of the delegates at the party convention.  

Any candidate who clears those hurdles ends up buried under big-money attacks that drown out whatever ideas they hoped to share, ideas I would have wanted to hear.  I don't blame people from not even trying.

I’m not asking for a better Republican or a different Democrat. I’m asking that any individual in my community, with or without a party, have a realistic path onto the ballot.

The first steps aren’t complicated. Lower signature thresholds. Draw districts that produce real competition. And adopt a basic democratic standard: every public office on the ballot should offer voters at least two candidates.

You and I may disagree about taxes, immigration, health care, and nearly everything else. That’s democracy. But we should be able to agree on the one thing that makes every other disagreement worth having: real choice.

Public office belongs to the public. Anyone qualified, willing, and motivated should have a fair shot at it. That is what democracy requires, and it is what we don’t have.

Why that doesn't make everyone drop everything they're doing, and move to change it, is beyond me.

⚠️ 🇺🇸 😷 Long COVID Recovery Remains Uneven as New Study Underscores Limits of Symptom Improvement

A prospective NIH-funded RECOVER study tracking 1,019 adults with probable Long COVID one year after infection reports that about half achieved sustained symptom improvement and roughly a quarter reached complete remission by three years, yet wide variation by symptom pattern and methodological constraints on recovery definitions show that lasting recovery is incomplete for many and that high-quality respirators remain the most reliable tool for preventing further cases.

Researchers from Massachusetts General Hospital and colleagues, publishing in Annals of Internal Medicine, used the Long COVID Research Index to follow participants. By three years after initial infection, 50.1 percent experienced sustained improvement defined as scores remaining below the likely-Long-COVID threshold at two successive visits roughly three months apart, while 26.9 percent reached complete remission. Outcomes differed sharply by subtype. People whose illness centered on smell or taste changes improved at rates near 60 percent, whereas those with multisystem symptoms saw sustained improvement in fewer than one in five cases. Bloomberg and other outlets covering the findings noted the same overall figures while highlighting the poorer trajectory for the more severe, multi-organ presentations.

Advocacy groups and clinicians have pointed to limitations in how recovery was measured. The index tracks a limited set of symptoms rather than the full range of Long COVID manifestations, and a single low-score visit can count as remission even if symptoms later return. Assessments every few months can miss fluctuating courses, post-exertional malaise, or functional declines that occur when patients reduce activity to manage crashes. Missing follow-up data, if more severe cases disproportionately withdrew, could further bias improvement estimates upward. These critiques do not invalidate the longitudinal data but illustrate why headline rates of 50 percent improvement should not be read as evidence that most people recover fully or that the condition is self-limiting for the majority.

The findings reinforce a practical public-health reality: prevention of initial infection and reinfection remains the clearest way to reduce the burden. SARS-CoV-2 spreads through the air, and laboratory and observational work consistently shows that well-fitting high-quality respirators—N95, KN95, FFP2, FFP3 or P100—filter at least 95 percent of infectious particles and outperform surgical or cloth masks for both source control and personal protection. A controlled exhaled-breath study found a duckbill N95 reduced viral aerosol shedding by 98 percent, far exceeding other face coverings. Continuous use in healthcare and higher-risk community settings has been linked to lower transmission. While any mask offers some benefit during periods of elevated respiratory virus activity, the superior filtration and seal of certified respirators provide the strongest individual and collective protection against the airborne pathogen that continues to drive new Long COVID cases.

Even under the study’s own metrics, half the cohort did not reach meaningful sustained improvement and two-thirds did not achieve full remission. Combined with the documented risks of reinfection worsening or triggering Long COVID, these numbers make the case for routine use of high-quality respirators in shared indoor spaces, healthcare settings, and during outbreaks. Collective adherence to such measures protects the most vulnerable without depending on incomplete recovery rates or questionnaire thresholds that can understate ongoing disability.

Several U.S. Senate races on the outer edge of the battleground map are now underway, including contests in Florida and South Carolina (where Republicans are favored) as well as Georgia and New Hampshire (where Democrats are favored). An unexpectedly competitive race in any of these states would be a significant development, potentially reshaping expectations for the rest of the night.

My first look, however, will at Florida U.S. House races.

Florida counts its votes exceptionally quickly, and we should begin seeing calls in competitive House districts relatively soon. These results will offer an early indication of the national environment, but with an important caveat: Florida has shifted steadily rightward and was a relative bright spot for Republicans in 2020, 2022, and 2024. Limited Democratic gains in Florida would not necessarily indicate a similarly weak performance nationally.

Three Democratic wins out of FL-07, FL-09, FL-14, FL-22, FL-25, and FL-27 would be a great start to the night for them. If Republicans were to win all six, control of the U.S. House would be very much in play.

We're also watching two major governor races: Keisha Lance Bottoms vs. Rick Jackson in Georgia and David Jolly vs. Byron Donalds in Florida.

One other place to watch closely is Loudoun County, Virginia. Its initial returns in 2024 were among the first signs that Kamala Harris was headed for a more difficult night than expected.

If the first hour gave us a glimpse of some initial results, but this is when we should begin learning something meaningful about the national picture.

As a reminder, statewide races in Florida and New Hampshire will not be callable until 8 p.m. ET when the final polls close in the state.

text:
On Being American

Between James Baldwin and Abdul 
@AbdulElSayed 

In 1959, James Baldwin wrote that discovering what it means to be American might begin with leaving America. Few American writers have meant more to me. He went to Paris fleeing a racism he feared would reduce the whole of his existence to the fact of his being Black, and confine his writing within the same narrow boundary. He wanted to discover how the particular truth of his experience might connect him to other people. In Paris, he wrote some of his finest essays, among them this one, which I have long loved.

In Europe, Baldwin discovered that Americans, whatever their ancestry or colour, carried a common history and wrestled with related questions of identity and belonging. Distance allowed him to see his country and to recognise what it had written into him. I understand something of this as an Egyptian. From a distance, the country becomes more legible; one begins to make out its lines, however faint they have grown.

For Baldwin, the great novelist and poet, life in Paris brought a measure of release from having to justify his vocation, and from the relentless anxiety of establishing his place in the world. Among people whose lives differed from his own, convictions he had scarcely known he possessed began to give way. He could return to his childhood, recover his voice, and bring back into the light memories he had buried.

Yet Europe did not distribute its freedoms equally. What an American enjoyed might be denied an Algerian on the very same street. No country stood outside injustice, and exile offered no exemption from responsibility.

Baldwin understood that a writer cannot erase his origins, and that growing into his powers requires coming to terms with them. His task is to uncover the hidden laws and unspoken assumptions by which a society lives, and to question the myths that keep it from knowing itself. The inward life has consequences. Dreams, however intangible they seem, leave their marks upon the world.

Writing thus becomes a responsibility to the truth: to examine the distance between America’s promises and the lives its people actually lead, and to discover what remains possible in a country still struggling to recognise its own face.

And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed is asking us, in his own way, to confront that same question: what does it mean to be American?

ELECTION DAY WATCH 2026 | REPORT 21

ARIZONA: FLOOD-DAMAGED ROADS THREATEN VOTING ACCESS IN NAVAJO NATION COMMUNITY

UPDATE: NOVEMBER 3, 2026

Severe flooding across parts of the Navajo Nation has damaged roads and bridges, creating serious Election Day access problems for residents of Rock Point, Arizona.

Local officials say the damage has made reaching polling locations extremely difficult.

WHAT HAS BEEN DOCUMENTED

ROCK POINT: APPROXIMATELY 600 VOTERS AT RISK

Rock Point Chapter Vice President Valinda Shirley told KNAU that flood-damaged roads could prevent roughly 600 Native American voters from reaching a polling location.

She reported that roads west of the community were largely impassable, although Highway 191 had reopened.

The 600 figure is an estimate of voters facing access problems.

It is NOT a confirmed count of people who were unable to vote.

ALTERNATIVE VOTING CENTERS

Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes pointed to voting centers in:

• Round Rock, approximately 17 miles away.
• Many Farms, approximately 34 miles away.

Shirley said those alternatives did not solve the immediate problem for residents unable to travel through damaged roads.

Some community members reportedly planned to walk to vote.

SEPARATE NAVAJO NATION ELECTION NOTICE

The Navajo Nation issued a notice identifying the Rock Point Chapter Administration Building as a polling location for its November 3 tribal general election.

That is a separate election from Arizona’s state and federal contests.

The notice does not establish that flooding caused the location change or that state-election polling sites were relocated.

TRANSPORTATION AND STATE RESPONSE

Shirley described local discussions about possible transportation assistance, including specialized vehicles capable of crossing difficult terrain.

Those discussions do not establish that transportation was actually provided.

The Arizona Secretary of State’s Office said it had contacted the Apache County Recorder and offered available resources.

Officials acknowledged that travel was difficult and directed residents to local authorities for transportation assistance.

WHAT REMAINS UNKNOWN

• How many eligible voters ultimately could not reach a polling location.
• Whether emergency transportation was successfully arranged.
• Whether any voting deadlines or locations were changed because of the flooding.
• Whether any voters ultimately lost the opportunity to cast a ballot.

BOTTOM LINE

Flooding created documented voting-access problems in a rural Native American community on Election Day.

Providing alternative voting centers does not necessarily resolve the problem when residents cannot reach them.

The final impact on turnout and voting access remains unknown.

Election officials should document the affected communities, transportation assistance provided, and any voting opportunities lost.

SOURCES:
• KNAU / KJZZ, November 3
• Rock Point Chapter Vice President Valinda Shirley
• Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes
• Arizona Secretary of State’s Office
• Navajo Nation official election-location notice, November 3

text:
The Flying Dorito🔺 (4k image)

Nicknamed ‘The Flying Dorito’ because of its shape, the A-12 Avenger II could have brought the capabilities of a stealth bomber to an aircraft carrier deck. But cost overruns and engineers’ failure to resolve technical problems saw the project cancelled amid controversy which still remains a quarter of a century later. AFM’s Glenn Sands looks at what might have been...

THE US Navy’s A-12 Avenger II Advanced Technology Aircraft (ATA) was proposed by McDonnell Douglas and General Dynamics as an all-weather, carrier-based stealth bomber to replace the Grumman A-6E Intruder in the mid-1990s.

Plans called for the A-12 to incorporate more advanced stealthy characteristics than the F-117A and carry a significantly greater payload. Some 620 were to have served with USN, and 228 in USMC squadrons – and at one time the USAF considered buying 400 to replace the F-111. Estimated cost per aircraft was $100m.

The A-12 was designed to fly faster and further than the Intruder and carry its weapon load internally to reduce drag and maintain a low RCS. Being a later generation aircraft, it was expected to be more reliable than the Intruder and need half the maintenance man-hours when deployed aboard a carrier.

But it proved to be the most troublesome of the new American stealth aircraft, owing to extensive use of composites on the airframe. The materials did not yield the anticipated weight savings, and some structural sections had to be replaced with heavier metal components, meaning each aircraft exceeding its weight by 30 tons – 30% more than its design specification and close to the limits that could be accommodated on USN aircraft carriers.

Additional problems were discovered with the Avenger II’s complex Inverse Synthetic Aperture Radar system, which was linked to its advanced avionics components, neither of which ‘talked’ to one another during testing.

At the time of Defense Secretary Dick Cheney’s Major Aircraft Review in late 1990, the full scope of the problems had not been revealed to the review board. The only decisions made were to slow the rate of production and drop the numbers planned for the USMC, which left the USN with a bill for the original 620. Cheney also decided to delay the Air Force purchase, planned for between 1992 and 1998, for more than five years.

Shortly after, contractors on the A-12 programme publicly revealed it was facing serious engineering problems and a 2bn cost overrun, which would delay the maiden flight by more than a year (to late 1991) and substantially raise the unit cost per aircraft.

The added weight meant the A-12’s performance offered little improvement over existing aircraft then flying from carrier decks, although backers of the programme claimed its stealth characteristics meant it would fly ‘invisible’, so a loss in performance was irrelevant.

As the cost of the programme spiralled and the radar problems continued, it was estimated that simply resolving the issues would consume up to 70% of the Navy’s budget for the aircraft. Following a design review completed in October 1990, the A-12’s first flight was rescheduled to early 1992. In December 1990, it was envisaged that 14 Navy aircraft carriers were to be equipped with a wing of 20 Avenger IIs each. But a government report released a few weeks before these announcements said serious problems remained with the development of the aircraft and the project faced a 2bn cost overrun.

In December 1990, Cheney told the Navy to justify the programme and deliver reasons why it should not be cancelled. Its response, and that of the contractors, failed to persuade him not to cancel the project – and on January 7, 1991 the entire A-12 Avenger II programme was terminated.

The US Government believed the contractors could not complete the A-12 and instructed them to repay most of the 2bn spent on its development – but McDonnell Douglas and General Dynamics disputed the demand in a federal court. The reasons for the cancellation have been debated ever since and remain controversial for those involved in the development of The Flying Dorito.

Illustrations and captions — pages 84–85
An artist’s concept showing Avenger II in operational service with the US Navy was released to the media so the general public could see the extraordinary shape of the carrier-based bomber.

During the development of the A-12, the two companies involved produced several adverts that were published across the aerospace press. It was an attempt to gain public backing for the aircraft.

Technical sidebar — pages 86–87
Engines: The aircraft was to be powered by two General Electric F412-GE-DF5F2 non-afterburning turbofan engines – each producing about 13,500lb of thrust – buried deep in the fuselage and fitted with mesh across the intake ducting similar to that used on the F-117A Nighthawk. Ironically, a General Electric F414 turbofan engine now powers the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet – a modified variant of the upgraded F412 version developed for the A-12.

Cockpit: The large single-piece canopy hinged to the right afforded the crew exceptional in-flight visibility. The pilot and bombardier/navigator sat in tandem, as on the F-14 Tomcat. The cockpit was described by those working on the programme as similar in layout to the F-15E Strike Eagle’s, with seven Kaiser multi-function displays (MFDs) divided between the front and rear compartments. The front cockpit was equipped with a Kaiser wide-field view holographic head-up display, which displayed information directly from the Westinghouse AN/APQ-183 multi-mode radar onto the screen in front of the pilot.

Armament: The A-12 was armed with two AIM-120 Advanced Medium Range Air-to-Air Missiles (AMRAAMs) for self-defence. The concealed weapons bays could carry two AGM-88 High-Speed Anti-Radiation Missiles (HARMs) and a full complement of air-to-ground ordnance, including unguided and precision-guided bombs. Allowances were made for the A-12 to deliver nuclear weapons from its internal bomb bay. It had a weapons load of 5,160lb.

Sneeky Pete: Evidence suggests the A-12 Avenger II concept was derived from an earlier, smaller stealth prototype called ‘Sneeky Pete’ (see Stealthy Secrets on the Shoulder, p96-97), which was designed to test the stealth flying wing penetrator concept in the early 1980s. It’s not clear if a classified Sneeky Pete actually flew as a technology demonstrator during the 1980s, but many aviation analysts believe it did, for a short trial period, from the Groom Lake Test Site. If actually tested, it has yet to be declassified.

Wings: A substantial wing fold mechanism at the midway point of the A-12’s wingspan enabled the aircraft to equal the stowage space of the A-6 Intruder, the jet it was to replace.

Illustration caption — pages 86–87
The A-12 Avenger II was to be the US Navy’s new Advanced Tactical Aircraft, designed to replace the A-6 Intruder.

Inyo County Names Bouchard Next CAO

With a contract approved at today’s meeting, Inyo County is poised to officially welcome Ms. Christine Bouchard as the next County Administrative Officer. The Board of Supervisors made a conditional offer of employment to Bouchard on October 13. Her start date will be November 12.

Bouchard’s appointment follows an extensive, comprehensive effort to recruit for a permanent CAO since late 2025.

“Christine brings with her a wide breadth of experience in county government and a proven track record of innovative, effective, and supportive leadership,” said Board Chair Trina Orrill. “Her areas of expertise range from budgeting and financial insights to personnel, real property, project, and team management. We look forward to embarking with her on this exciting new chapter for Inyo County.”

Bouchard is no stranger to the Eastern Sierra. She served the last three years as Mono County’s Assistant County Administrative Officer, where she helped evaluate, formulate, and develop recommendations on improvements to county operations, programs, and services. Prior to that, Bouchard served as Administrative Services Manager for the Santa Cruz Port District, Administrative Services Manager for the County of Santa Cruz, and Senior Administrative Analyst for Amador County General Services.

A veteran of the U.S. Navy, Bouchard went on to receive her education in Business Management and Employment Law.

Bouchard said she is eager to step into this important role and get to know the Inyo County workforce that is the backbone of the organization.

“I am excited to build positive, productive, and lasting relationships with an already well-established team. I am bringing over 27 years of a combination of military, public service, and County Government time to the organization,” Bouchard said. “I am enthusiastic to put my experience, training, and knowledge to work to bring the County to the highest possible level. The health, safety, and well-being of the community will always be my highest priority. I believe that fiscal responsibility and transparency are essential in maintaining the trust and respect of the public. It is my honor and absolute privilege to start working for the people of Inyo County.”

text:
@DetroitRedWings  have massively screwed up the Dylan Larkin saga and they only continue to make it worse.

Detroit had a Dylan Larkin deal with Minnesota sitting on the table this summer, and they let it walk. Four months later their former captain is suspended without pay, the leverage is gone, and the market for him looks nothing like it did in July.

Go back to the offseason. The package being discussed was built around Danila Yurov and Charlie Stramel, with a first-round pick and another roster player added on top. Ryan Hartman was the name that kept surfacing as that extra piece, and depending on who you asked, Jonas Brodin, Yakov Trenin and maybe even Jesper Wallstedt. Either way, that's a 22-year-old center with top-six upside, a first-round prospect, draft capital, and an NHL regular. For a 30-year-old center who'd already asked out, that's a strong return, and Detroit passed on it.

The whole case for Larkin in Minnesota was that the Wild haven't had a true No. 1 center in years, dating back to Mikko Koivu. Coming into camp, the projected top line had Kaprizov with Yurov down the middle, and plenty of people expected Hartman to end up there at some point. Nobody was comfortable with that. Hartman's a useful player, but he's a third- or fourth-line center who brings energy and some sandpaper. He isn't the guy you build a first line around, and the Wild knew it. That gap is exactly what made Larkin such a clean fit.

Then the season started and John Hynes found the answer on his own roster. Kaprizov, Joel Eriksson Ek, and Matt Boldy have been the best line in hockey through 16 games, and the numbers aren't close. They're 14-1 in goals at 5-on-5 with a 68% expected goals share, and all three rank 1-2-3 in the entire league in individual expected goals. Eriksson Ek was supposed to be the second-line shutdown center. Instead he's centering the most dominant trio in the sport.

That changes everything about what Larkin is worth to Minnesota. He's no longer the missing 1C. He'd slot in on the second line between Blake Coleman and Maxim Shabanov. That's a very good second line, and it makes the Wild deeper. But a team doesn't pay a first-line price for a second-line upgrade, and Detroit is still asking like it's July.

Meanwhile the main piece in the deal has only gotten better. Yurov has 5 goals and 6 points through 16 games, a 26-goal pace at 22 years old, and he's in the 94th percentile in high-danger chance suppression. He's driving play at both ends, not just producing. Minnesota would still include him, but now he's the headliner instead of one piece of a bigger package. Detroit isn't getting Yurov plus Stramel plus a first plus a roster player anymore. That version of the deal expired when they decided to wait.

And the longer this drags, the more it looks personal. Larkin asked out as the long time captain, Detroit native, and Detroit seems determined to make him pay for it, even if it costs them on the return. Compare it to what Minnesota gave Vancouver for Quinn Hughes last December: Marco Rossi, Liam Öhgren, Zeev Buium, and a 2026 first. That was for arguably the best defenseman in the world. Detroit wants more than that for a 30-year-old who'd be a second-line center in Minnesota and is never playing another game for the Red Wings.

At some point the Red Wings front office has to accept that this summer's offer was the best one they were ever going to see. Every week they wait, the return gets smaller.

text:
“We all have the same 24 hours in a day" is not quite true.

The same trip four ways:
Driving: 22 minutes. 
Biking: 24 minutes.
Public transit: 2 hours and 54 minutes. 
Walking: almost 4 hours.

Same job, same shift. If you have a reliable car, that’s about 45 minutes a day round trip. If you don’t, it could be close to six hours, before you’ve worked a single minute.

Not every transit commute is that bad, and plenty of people have great bus or train options. But for a lot of families, this is real. It means leaving before sunrise, getting home after dark and trying to squeeze in dinner, homework and sleep in whatever’s left.

As a childcare center owner, I know how tight the window between work and pickup can be. A long commute makes that window even tighter. Time is a cost, even when it doesn’t show up on a bill.

And it’s often the people with the least money who lose the most time. That’s the frustrating part. Budgeting and hard work matter, but it’s a lot easier to get ahead when you aren’t spending half your free time just getting to work.

If you’re stuck in a long commute, a few things to consider:
~Ask your employer about remote days, flexible hours or a schedule that avoids rush hour.
~Check whether your employer offers pre-tax transit benefits, which can save you money on passes.
~When job hunting, count the commute as part of the pay. A job paying $2 more an hour can be a worse deal if it adds two hours a day.
~Look into reduced-fare programs. Here in the Denver area, RTD offers discounted fares for people with lower incomes.

Your time has value. Spend it like it does.

I’m not a financial advisor.

Sources: RTD, IRS Publication 15-B

text:
He was 12 when he killed his 6-year-old cousin. Prosecutors offered him 3 years in a juvenile facility. His mother turned it down.

At 14, Lionel Tate became the youngest American ever sentenced to life in prison without parole.

July 28, 1999, Broward County, Florida. His mother was babysitting Tiffany Eunick. The two kids were downstairs, watching wrestling on TV.

About 45 minutes later, he came upstairs and said Tiffany wasn't breathing.

She weighed 48 pounds. He weighed 170. The medical examiner counted more than 35 injuries, including a fractured skull.

His lawyer said he was copying wrestling moves. The press called it the "wrestling defense." Hulk Hogan, Sting and The Rock were subpoenaed. The judge ruled they didn't have to come.

According to the prosecution, the day after Tiffany died he asked her mother if he could have her toys.

The prosecutor, Ken Padowitz, offered the same 3-year deal again and again, right up until trial. It was rejected every time.

In the video below, the jury's verdict is read in court: "guilty of murder in the first degree." Then the prosecutor who won the case says he thought the sentence was wrong.

"I made no secret by the fact that I found life in prison with no parole inappropriate."

An appeals court threw out the conviction. Padowitz put the deal back on the table: "the same exact plea offer that I had engineered three years earlier." Tate, now 16, took it and went home on house arrest and probation.

In May 2005 he was arrested for robbing a Domino's delivery man at gunpoint. He got 30 years for violating his probation.

Was Lionel Tate a child the system failed, or did he get two chances and throw them away?

Uh huh.... California had the same pitch. How has that shaken out?

Let's check.. (and pay attention to the final bit on projected vs. actual cost)

The California High-Speed Rail (CAHSR) project is an under-construction, publicly funded high-speed rail network managed by the California High-Speed Rail Authority. Authorized by voters via Proposition 1A in 2008, the system aims to eventually link major regions of the state with trains capable of reaching speeds up to 220 mph (350 km/h). 

Project Scope and Phases

Phase 1 (Bay Area to Greater Los Angeles): Spans roughly 494 miles (795 km), designed to offer a non-stop express connection between San Francisco and Los Angeles in 2 hours and 40 minutes. [1]
Phase 2 (Extensions): Plans extend the system north to Sacramento and south to San Diego, bringing the total proposed network to 776–800 miles with up to 24 stations. 

Initial Operating Segment (IOS): Active construction is currently concentrated on a 119-mile (171-mile broader footprint) stretch in the Central Valley connecting Merced, Fresno, and Bakersfield. 

Current Status and Timeline

Target Launch: Passenger operations for the initial segment are targeted to begin between 2031 and 2033, with the full Phase 1 buildout projected toward 2039–2040.

Leadership Transition: CEO Ian Choudri resigned in October 2026 following scrutiny and an Office of the Inspector General investigation into consultant travel expenses. Joe Stephenshaw, director of the California Department of Finance, was named interim CEO. 

Trainsets: The authority approved a contract with Siemens Mobility for initial high-speed trainsets, with testing expected to begin by early 2030. 

Construction Progress: Dozens of grade separations, overpasses, and structural viaducts (such as the Hanford Viaduct) have been completed across the Central Valley. 

Costs and Funding

Cost Escalation: Originally estimated around $33 billion to $45 billion in 2008, updated projections place the cost for Phase 1 between $126 billion and $231 billion. The 119-mile Central Valley segment alone is estimated at roughly $36 billion.

Funding Sources: Financed through a mix of state bond proceeds (Proposition 1A), state cap-and-trade greenhouse gas reduction funds, and federal grants.

Stephanie Nolen saw nine women bring new babies safely into the world while reporting this story in labor wards in the north of Nigeria.

The maternal drape, as it is called, is helping to solve one of the world’s most intractable health problems.

An 80-Cent Plastic Pouch Is Saving Thousands of Women From Dying in Childbirth

A few hours after she nearly bled to death, Husaina Balarabe was serenely unaware that her life had been in peril.

She cuddled her newborn baby, a lush-cheeked boy she had named Aabid, and showed him off to her sisters from her bed in a noisy hospital delivery ward in the northern Nigerian city of Kano.
